sections.name: Web Security & OWASP Top 10
sections.explanation_simple: Web security is about protecting websites and web apps from attackers. The OWASP Top 10 is the most important list of web security risks - think of it as 'the top 10 ways websites get hacked'. If you're building a web app, you MUST know these. The big ones are: SQL Injection (hackers can read your database), XSS (hackers can run JavaScript in your users' browsers), and CSRF (hackers can make your users do things without knowing). Each one has a simple fix once you know about it.
key_concepts: SQL Injection: Attacker puts SQL code in input fields to steal/modify database data
XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): Attacker injects JavaScript that runs in other users' browsers
CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): Attacker tricks users into performing actions unknowingly
SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery): Attacker makes server send requests to internal systems
IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): Accessing other users' data by changing an ID number
CSP (Content Security Policy): HTTP header that prevents XSS
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): Controls which websites can access your API
Rate Limiting: Blocking IPs that make too many requests (prevents brute force)
Input Validation: Never trust user input - ALWAYS validate and sanitize

code_examples.title: SQL Injection Demonstration (Educational)
code_examples.code:
# EDUCATIONAL EXAMPLE - Understanding SQL injection for defense
# NEVER try these on any system without permission

"""
HOW SQL INJECTION WORKS:

A vulnerable login query:
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='[INPUT]' AND password='[INPUT]'

Normal input: username = "alice", password = "secret123"
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='alice' AND password='secret123'
  -> Returns Alice's record (if password matches)

Malicious input: username = "admin' --", password = "anything"
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin' --' AND password='anything'
  -> The -- comments out the password check!
  -> Returns admin's record WITHOUT knowing the password

Even worse: username = "'; DROP TABLE users; --"
  -> Deletes the entire users table!
"""

# HOW TO DEFEND: Use parameterized queries (NEVER string concatenation)

# VULNERABLE (DON'T DO THIS):
def login_vulnerable(username, password):
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='{username}' AND password='{password}'"
    # If username = "admin' --", this becomes:
    # SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin' --' AND password='...'
    # The attacker is logged in as admin!
    return execute_query(query)

# SECURE (DO THIS INSTEAD):
def login_secure(username, password):
    query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?"
    # The database treats username and password as DATA, not code
    # Even if username = "admin' --", it's treated as a literal string
    return execute_parameterized_query(query, (username, password))

# In Python with SQLite:
import sqlite3

def secure_login(db_path, username, password):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    # NEVER DO THIS:
    # cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='{username}'")
    
    # ALWAYS DO THIS (parameterized query):
    cursor.execute(
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?",
        (username, password)
    )
    
    return cursor.fetchone()

# DEFENSE SUMMARY:
# 1. Use parameterized queries (or ORM) - ALWAYS
# 2. Validate input types (is it a number? string? email?)
# 3. Least privilege - database account should only be able to read/write what it needs
# 4. WAF (Web Application Firewall) for extra protection layer
print("SQL Injection educational example loaded.")
print("Defense: Always use parameterized queries, never string concatenation.")

Reflected XSS: Script in URL, reflected back in response (e.g., search) 3. DOM-based XSS: Client-side JavaScript modifies DOM unsafely Example attack (stored): User posts a comment with: When anyone views the comment, their cookies are stolen! """ # DEFENSE - Content Security Policy (CSP) # Set this HTTP header to prevent XSS: # Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.com def set_csp_headers(response): """Set security headers to prevent XSS.""" response.headers['Content-Security-Policy'] = \ "default-src 'self'; " \ "script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; " \ "style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; " \ "img-src 'self' data: https:; " \ "font-src 'self' https://fonts.googleapis.com; " \ "object-src 'none'; " \ "frame-ancestors 'none'; " \ "base-uri 'self'" response.headers['X-Content-Type-Options'] = 'nosniff' response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = 'DENY' response.headers['X-XSS-Protection'] = '1; mode=block' response.headers['Referrer-Policy'] = 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' return response # DEFENSE - Output Encoding (escape user content before displaying) import html def display_comment(comment_text): """Safely display user-generated content.""" # html.escape converts < to < and > to > # This prevents the browser from treating it as HTML/JavaScript safe_text = html.escape(comment_text) return f"

sections.name: Cryptography & Network Security
sections.explanation_simple: Cryptography is the art of keeping secrets in a digital world. It's how your browser talks securely to websites (HTTPS), how WhatsApp messages are kept private, and how passwords are stored safely. There are two main types: symmetric encryption (same key to lock and unlock, like a house key) and asymmetric encryption (two different keys - one public to lock, one private to unlock, like a mailbox). Hashing is different - it's a one-way process that can't be reversed, used for storing passwords and verifying data integrity.
key_concepts: Symmetric Encryption: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) - fast, same key to encrypt/decrypt
Asymmetric Encryption: RSA, ECC - public/private key pair, used for HTTPS
Hashing: SHA-256, bcrypt - one-way, can't be reversed (password storage)
HTTPS/TLS: The protocol that secures web traffic (padlock in browser)
Certificate: Proves a website is who it says it is
Digital Signature: Proves a message came from you and wasn't changed
Perfect Forward Secrecy: Past messages stay secret even if key is compromised
Zero Trust: Never trust, always verify (modern security model)

code_examples.title: Python Cryptography Examples (Educational)
code_examples.code:
# EDUCATIONAL - Cryptography examples for understanding security

from cryptography.fernet import Fernet
import hashlib
import bcrypt

# 1. SYMMETRIC ENCRYPTION (AES)
# Same key encrypts and decrypts
print("=== SYMMETRIC ENCRYPTION (AES) ===")

# Generate a key
key = Fernet.generate_key()
cipher = Fernet(key)

# Encrypt a message
message = b"This is secret game data"
encrypted = cipher.encrypt(message)
print(f"Original: {message}")
print(f"Encrypted: {encrypted}")

# Decrypt
decrypted = cipher.decrypt(encrypted)
print(f"Decrypted: {decrypted}")
print(f"Key (SAVE THIS!): {key}")
print()

# 2. PASSWORD HASHING (bcrypt)
# One-way - can't get password back from hash
# Slow by design (to prevent brute force)
print("=== PASSWORD STORAGE (bcrypt) ===")

password = b"my_secure_password123"

# Hash password (salt is automatically included)
hash = bcrypt.hashpw(password, bcrypt.gensalt())
print(f"Password: {password}")
print(f"Hash: {hash}")

# Check password (verify against stored hash)
entered_password = b"my_secure_password123"
is_correct = bcrypt.checkpw(entered_password, hash)
print(f"Password correct: {is_correct}")

entered_password_wrong = b"wrong_password"
is_correct = bcrypt.checkpw(entered_password_wrong, hash)
print(f"Wrong password correct: {is_correct}")
print()

# 3. HASHING for data integrity
# SHA-256 produces a fixed-size fingerprint of data
print("=== DATA INTEGRITY (SHA-256) ===")

data = b"This save file should not be tampered with"
checksum = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
print(f"Data: {data}")
print(f"SHA-256: {checksum}")

# Even a small change produces a completely different hash
data2 = b"This save file should not be tampered with."  # Added period
checksum2 = hashlib.sha256(data2).hexdigest()
print(f"\nData2: {data2}")
print(f"SHA-256: {checksum2}")
print(f"Hashes match: {checksum == checksum2}")

print("\nDefense summary:")
print("- Use bcrypt/argon2 for passwords (NOT MD5 or SHA)")
print("- Use TLS for all network traffic")
print("- Use encryption at rest for sensitive data")
print("- Hash important files to detect tampering")
